power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .5 ", Sentence = "We excluded participants whose rule-judgment accuracy did not exceed chance, defined as a one-sided exact binomial test against p = .5 across all 360 trials (α = .05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Cognitive resources are limited, yet people face an abundance of information.
Often, which information matters is not stated and can change over time, so people must learn it through experience.
This creates a tradeoff: uncertainty requires broad maintenance of multiple information sources, whereas certainty allows resources to be allocated more selectively.
Does this reorganization of resources reflect enhancement of relevant information, degradation of irrelevant information, or both?
Working memory provides a window into this process because differences in attentional priority should be reflected in what is remembered.

To address these questions, we developed the Continuously Assessed Rule Inference Task, in which participants (N = 104) judged whether multidimensional stimuli followed a hidden rule that changed without warning, requiring them to continually update their beliefs about which information was relevant.
On intermittent probe trials, participants reproduced the color, shape, and motion direction of the preceding stimulus.
A reinforcement-learning model estimated trial-by-trial rule certainty from participants' choices.
As certainty increased, rule judgments relied more on evidence from the rule-defining (active) dimension, and memory for inactive features declined.
A mixture model showed that active features became more likely to be retained, and inactive features less likely, with little evidence that the precision of retained features changed.
These findings suggest that learning what matters reorganizes working memory by changing which information is retained, rather than how precisely it is represented.
This shift from broad to selective maintenance may reflect a tradeoff between flexibility under uncertainty and efficiency once relevant information has been identified.
Adaptive behavior requires us not only to attend to relevant information, but also to learn which information is relevant in the first place.
For example, when buying food for a newly adopted cat, you first must weigh several factors, such as flavor and texture, because you do not yet know what he prefers.
But once you learn that he consistently prefers salmon, you can scan for that ingredient and ignore the rest.
Many everyday tasks share this structure, where what matters is not directly stated but must be inferred from feedback (Badre et al., 2010; Karagoz et al., 2025; Wilson & Niv, 2011).
text.formatted: Many everyday tasks share this structure, where what matters is not directly stated but must be inferred from feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Badre et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Karagoz et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Wilson & Niv, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In these situations, a key challenge is to allocate limited cognitive resources across potentially relevant sources of information, and the optimal allocation should depend on how certain we are about what matters.
Yet it remains unclear how inferred relevance shapes how people process and retain information in working memory.

One natural way to go about dividing cognitive resources is to allocate them broadly while relevance is uncertain, preserving evidence for evaluating and contrasting alternatives, and selectively once certainty grows, reducing the cost of maintaining information (Marshall & Bays, 2013).
text.formatted: One natural way to go about dividing cognitive resources is to allocate them broadly while relevance is uncertain, preserving evidence for evaluating and contrasting alternatives, and selectively once certainty grows, reducing the cost of maintaining information <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Marshall & Bays, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This allocation must be reconfigured when relevance changes, broadening again before narrowing on the newly relevant information (Egner, 2023; Monsell, 2003).
text.formatted: This allocation must be reconfigured when relevance changes, broadening again before narrowing on the newly relevant information <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Egner, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Monsell, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Studies of learning and attention support this idea.
In associative learning, attention is distributed across multiple cues when outcomes are uncertain and concentrates on the most predictive cue once it becomes reliable (Walker et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In associative learning, attention is distributed across multiple cues when outcomes are uncertain and concentrates on the most predictive cue once it becomes reliable <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Walker et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: When previously reliable cues stop predicting outcomes, renewed uncertainty broadens attention across cues again, facilitating learning of new associations (Easdale et al., 2019).
text.formatted: When previously reliable cues stop predicting outcomes, renewed uncertainty broadens attention across cues again, facilitating learning of new associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Easdale et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, in multidimensional learning, attention shifts toward dimensions with higher learned value (Leong et al., 2017; Niv et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Similarly, in multidimensional learning, attention shifts toward dimensions with higher learned value <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Leong et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Niv et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies only measure how attention is deployed, focusing on gaze patterns or which dimensions drive choice, but not subsequently remembered for inference.
Attending to a stimulus feature does not guarantee it is maintained in memory, and attending away from it does not guarantee that it is forgotten.
Working memory offers a window onto the distribution of cognitive resources across information sources.

Explicit signals about goal relevance shape how information is encoded in working memory (Klyszejko et al., 2014; Krawczyk et al., 2007), through the strengthening of relevant information and the suppression of irrelevant information (Gazzaley & Nobre, 2012; Myers et al., 2017; Zanto & Gazzaley, 2009).
text.formatted: Explicit signals about goal relevance shape how information is encoded in working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Klyszejko et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Krawczyk et al., 2007)</ref>, through the strengthening of relevant information and the suppression of irrelevant information <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Gazzaley & Nobre, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Myers et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Zanto & Gazzaley, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Such modulation can also occur after encoding: directing attention to information already held in working memory improves memory for it relative to competing representations (Griffin & Nobre, 2003; Gunseli et al., 2015; Souza & Oberauer, 2016).
text.formatted: Such modulation can also occur after encoding: directing attention to information already held in working memory improves memory for it relative to competing representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Griffin & Nobre, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gunseli et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Souza & Oberauer, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: It is not obvious whether the same holds when relevance is not explicitly cued but must be inferred.

Attending to an object often brings its task-irrelevant features into working memory (Luck & Vogel, 1997), although these features are represented less precisely than relevant ones (LaRocque et al., 2017; Shin & Ma, 2016).
text.formatted: Attending to an object often brings its task-irrelevant features into working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Luck & Vogel, 1997)</ref>, although these features are represented less precisely than relevant ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(LaRocque et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Shin & Ma, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Combined with evidence that cued priority modulates working memory precision (Klyszejko et al., 2014), this suggests that learned relevance may redistribute precision across features while leaving all in memory.
text.formatted: Combined with evidence that cued priority modulates working memory precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Klyszejko et al., 2014)</ref>, this suggests that learned relevance may redistribute precision across features while leaving all in memory.

text.text: Alternatively, features that are not expected to be needed can be lost almost immediately (Chen & Wyble, 2015).
text.formatted: Alternatively, features that are not expected to be needed can be lost almost immediately <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chen & Wyble, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Under this account, relevance acts as a gate on what information is maintained.
Critically, these possibilities can be distinguished by using continuous-report tasks, asking participants to reproduce a presented feature value (Wilken & Ma, 2004).
text.formatted: Critically, these possibilities can be distinguished by using continuous-report tasks, asking participants to reproduce a presented feature value <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Wilken & Ma, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The continuous errors that arise from this procedure can be modeled as a mixture of memory-based responses and random guesses, separating the probability that feature values are maintained from the precision of their representations (Bays et al., 2009; Souza et al., 2016; Zhang & Luck, 2008).
text.formatted: The continuous errors that arise from this procedure can be modeled as a mixture of memory-based responses and random guesses, separating the probability that feature values are maintained from the precision of their representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bays et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Souza et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Zhang & Luck, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: If working memory shifts from broad to selective maintenance with increasing certainty, memory for relevant information should improve relative to memory for irrelevant features.
If this shift reflects a redistribution of resources, the divergence should appear primarily in precision.
If it reflects gating, it should appear primarily in the probability that features are retained.

To address these questions, we developed the Continuously Assessed Rule Inference Task (CARIT), adapted from a paradigm developed by Karagoz and colleagues (2025) which was itself modeled after the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (Berg, 1948).
text.formatted: To address these questions, we developed the Continuously Assessed Rule Inference Task (CARIT), adapted from a paradigm developed by <ref type="bibr">Karagoz and colleagues (2025)</ref> which was itself modeled after the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Berg, 1948)</ref>.

text.text: On each trial, participants judged whether a stimulus, defined by three features varying along continuous circular spaces (color, shape, and motion direction), conformed to a hidden rule on one of these dimensions (e.g., whether its color was cool).
Because the rule switched unpredictably, participants had to repeatedly infer which dimension mattered.
A reinforcement-learning model (RL) fit to participants' choices provided trial-by-trial estimates of their certainty about which rule was active.

Intermittent probes asked participants to reconstruct all three features of the preceding stimulus, allowing us to track how memory for features on the active dimension (defining the current rule) and the inactive dimensions) changed as rule certainty evolved.
We then used a mixture model of report errors to test whether any divergence between memory for active and inactive features reflected changes in retention probability, precision, or both.
We recruited 137 participants from the student population of Washington University in St.
Louis.
Participants received academic course credit through participation.
All participants completed the experiment in person and provided informed consent before starting.
All procedures were approved by the Washington University in St.
Louis Institutional Review Board.
We excluded participants whose rule-judgment accuracy did not exceed chance, defined as a one-sided exact binomial test against p = .5 across all 360 trials (α = .05).
This corresponds to a minimum accuracy of 54.7%.
Thirty-three participants fell below this threshold, leaving a final sample of 104 (mean age = 19.23 years, 76 women, 28 men, 0 non-binary).

To assess goal inference and working memory concurrently, participants completed the Continuously Assessed Rule Inference Task (CARIT; Figure 1), programmed in jsPsych (de Leeuw, 2015) using the RDK plugin (Rajananda et al., 2017).

text.text: On each trial, participants viewed a field of 20 color-filled shapes moving coherently across a circular aperture.

Colors were drawn from a circle in CIELAB space (L* = 50, a* = 20, b* = 20, radius = 60; Wilken & Ma, 2004), shapes from the Validated Circular Shape space, in which perceptual similarity decreases with angular distance (Li et al., 2020), and motion directions from the full 360° range.

text.text: Feature values were initially sampled independently and uniformly from their respective circles.
On the first trial after a rule switch, if the previous and new rules implied the same response, we resampled only the feature relevant to the new rule until the two rules implied opposite responses.
This ensured that participants who continued to apply the previous rule received incorrect feedback.
On each trial, participants judged whether the current stimulus conforms to a hidden rule (Figure 1B) by pressing the "Y" or "N" key within a response window of 5000 ms.

text.text: They then received feedback on correctness for 2000 ms.
Trials were separated by an intertrial interval of 500 ms.
The active rule was not cued, so participants had to infer it from feedback.
The rule switched without warning every 9 to 11 trials (uniformly sampled), producing 36 rule blocks across 360 trials.
At each switch, the new rule was randomly selected from the four rules along the two dimensions not shared by the current rule.

To assess how features were maintained, working memory probes followed the rule judgment on 36 of the 360 trials, yielding an average of one probe every 10 trials with the constraint that no two consecutive trials were probed.
Each sequence of probes began with a pause symbol, signaling that the rule-judgment task was suspended and that the probes would not affect the active rule.

After a 1000 ms delay, participants reconstructed the color, shape, and motion direction of the just-seen stimulus using three continuous response wheels (Li et al., 2020; Wilken & Ma, 2004), presented in random order.

text.text: Clicking or dragging on a wheel displayed a preview of the selected feature value.
After responding to all three probes, a play symbol then signaled that the rule-judgment task resumed.
Because probes were distributed throughout rule blocks, they sampled working memory at different stages of rule inference.
Participants viewed stimuli defined by three continuous dimensions: color, shape, and motion.
On each trial, they judged whether the stimulus conformed to a hidden active rule and received binary feedback on their correctness.
Intermittent WM probes were placed randomly throughout the task to assess WM representation for all three dimensions of the previously seen stimulus.
Each probe was preceded by a pause symbol and followed by a play symbol, signaling that the probe did not change the active rule.
Participants responded on feature response wheels to reconstruct the color, shape, and motion of the previous stimulus.

Before the main task, participants received extensive instructions.
After exposure to the stimuli, they were instructed on the six rules.
They then completed six practice trials for each rule, in which the rule was stated explicitly (e.g., "Does this stimulus follow the warm rule?").
Next, they performed three practice trials reproducing features on each of the three response wheels.
To characterize behavior on this task, we aligned trials to the first error following each switch, because this error provided the first evidence that the rule had changed.
For reaction time (RT) analyses, we excluded trials with no responses and RTs below 400 ms (totaling 3.0% of trials).

To distinguish rule-related slowing from general post-error slowing, we compared RTs on trials following the first error after a switch with RTs on trials following other errors, controlling for trial position.

Perceptual evidence on each trial was indexed by the circular distance between each feature value and its nearest category prototype (e.g., the warmest color), ranging from 0° (at the prototype) to 90° (at a category boundary), with larger distances indicating weaker evidence.
Error on the working memory probes was defined as the angular difference between the reported and presented feature value, ranging from -180° to 180°.

To validate the certainty measure, we tested whether participants responded faster when they were more certain about the rule, and whether judgements became increasingly sensitive to goal-relevant evidence as certainty grew.

We next turned to our central question: how does inferred relevance shape the attentional priority structure of working memory?
If participants increasingly directed resources towards the active dimension as certainty grew, memory should increasingly favor the active dimension over the inactive dimensions.

This divergence reflected opposing patterns for active and inactive dimensions, with greater certainty predicting better memory for active dimensions (b = -4.35, 95% CI [-7.83, -0.90], ER = 143.6), and worse memory for inactive dimensions (b = 1.69, 95% CI [-0.73, 4.11], ER = 10.6).
This pattern suggests increasingly selective prioritization as participants became more certain about which dimension mattered.
The increasing selectivity of working memory in response to rule certainty can reflect distinct mechanistic processes.
Increasing certainty could change whether features were retained, how precisely retained information was represented, or both.

To distinguish these possibilities, we fit a hierarchical Bayesian mixture model to signed report errors, in which certainty predicted both the probability of retaining a feature (𝑝 5 ) as well as the precision of retained features (𝜎), separately for active and inactive dimensions (Table S5, see Methods).

Thus, as certainty about which rule was active increased, the estimated probabilities of retaining goal-relevant and irrelevant information increasingly diverged, rising for the former and falling for the latter.

In contrast, there was little evidence that certainty affected how precisely retained information was represented for either active (b = -0.245, 95% CI [-3.73, 3.13], ER = 1.21) or inactive features (b = -0.141, 95% CI [-2.85, 2.51], ER = 1.18).

text.text: Thus, as participants became more certain about which rule was active, the selectivity of working memory was expressed primarily in which features were retained, rather than in how precisely they were represented.
Together, these analyses show that increasing certainty about which rule was active reshaped both the use and the retention of stimulus information, but in complementary ways.
Rule judgments came to rely more on evidence from the active dimension, whereas working memory increasingly lost features from the inactive dimensions.
In dynamic environments, people must often learn from experience which information is relevant, rather than relying on explicit instructions.
This requires a balance between maintaining broad access to potentially useful information and selectively allocating limited resources to what appears to matter.

Although prior work shows that attention becomes more selective during learning (Leong et al., 2017; Niv et al., 2015), it has remained unclear how this adjustment changes how people retain information in working memory.

text.text: We addressed this question using the CARIT, which combines continuous working memory reports with computational modeling, allowing us to track how memory for relevant and irrelevant features changed alongside participants' beliefs about which rule was active.
As model-derived certainty increased, rule judgments came to rely increasingly on evidence from the active dimension.

At the same time, working memory became increasingly selective, with memory for inactive features declining relative to memory for active features, suggesting a reorganization of the underlying priority structure.

Decomposing report errors showed that this selectivity primarily reflected whether features were retained rather than how precisely they were represented: as certainty grew, features on the relevant dimension became more likely to be retained, and features on irrelevant dimensions less likely.

These findings suggest that learning what matters is accompanied by a reorganization of the information maintained in working memory: as people become more certain about what matters, working memory increasingly retains goal-relevant information and drops competing information.
Our findings speak to how learned relevance shapes the content of working memory through the reorganization of attentional selection.
Attending to an object brings its taskirrelevant features into memory (Marshall & Bays, 2013), albeit with reduced precision (Shin & Ma, 2016).

text.text: Thus, one might expect that learned relevance redistributes resources across features, while leaving them all in memory.
Our results instead suggest that learned relevance primarily affects whether features are retained, rather than how precisely they represented.

As certainty grew, features on the active dimension became more likely to be retained and features on inactive dimensions less likely, with little evidence for changes in the precision of retained features.

This pattern is more consistent with learned relevance acting as a gate on what is retained, similar to the loss of attended but unneeded information observed in attribute amnesia (Chen & Wyble, 2015).

text.text: It also connects to accounts in which attention makes learning tractable by concentrating processing on a subset of relevant dimensions (Niv et al., 2015; Wilson & Niv, 2011), suggesting that this simplification extends beyond perceptual selection to the information maintained for subsequent use.

text.text: Here, this means that poorer memory for irrelevant features is useful for task performance, with attentional narrowing constraining which evidence remains accessible for evaluating alternative rules.
We found that during rule judgments, irrelevant information affected judgment speed, yet the same features became increasingly likely to be lost from working memory.
Thus, irrelevant information was processed without being retained.
Conversely, increased certainty enhanced the use of relevant information but only produced a modest gain in its retention.

This suggests that inferred relevance acts in different ways in different processing stages: during judgement, it increases the weight given to relevant evidence, while for storage it also determines whether irrelevant information is maintained at all.

A similar dissociation is found in attribute amnesia, where features that were attended and used for a task can nevertheless be lost immediately when they are not anticipated to be needed (Chen & Wyble, 2015).

text.text: It also has methodological implications.
Measures of attention during learning, such as gaze, are often used to infer which information people represent (Leong et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Measures of attention during learning, such as gaze, are often used to infer which information people represent <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Leong et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Walker et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Our results suggest that such measures may overestimate what is subsequently available in memory.
Our results also differ in an informative way from studies in which priority is explicitly cued.
When priority is cued before the stimulus is presented, it modulates the precision of working memory representations (Bays & Husain, 2008; Klyszejko et al., 2014).
text.formatted: When priority is cued before the stimulus is presented, it modulates the precision of working memory representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bays & Husain, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Klyszejko et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, when a retained feature in working memory is retro-cued, its representation becomes more precise (Park et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Similarly, when a retained feature in working memory is retro-cued, its representation becomes more precise <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Park et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, we found that learned relevance mainly affected whether features were retained, with little evidence for changes in precision.
One possibility is that this reflects participants' confidence about the utility of information.
In cuing studies, uncued information remains potentially relevant to the upcoming test (if only because researchers need invalid trials to measure the effect of cuing).
In the CARIT, irrelevant information can truly be dropped once certainty grows rather than degraded.
The transition from broad to selective maintenance suggests an exploration-exploitation interpretation of working memory prioritization.

Evidence from associative learning suggests that uncertainty promotes attentional exploration (Beesley et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2019), which can facilitate learning when previously uninformative cues become predictive (Easdale et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Evidence from associative learning suggests that uncertainty promotes attentional exploration <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beesley et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Walker et al., 2019)</ref>, which can facilitate learning when previously uninformative cues become predictive <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Easdale et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Our results extend this account to the information retained during inference, suggesting that exploration may involve preserving multiple sources of evidence in working memory as well as sampling them perceptually.
Under uncertainty, information outside the currently favored dimension could help evaluate alternative rules.
As certainty increases, retaining that information contributes less to the current judgment.

This suggests a reciprocal relationship between learning and working memory: beliefs about relevance shape what is retained, while what is retained shapes the evidence available for subsequent inference.
A narrowing of working memory organization therefore comes at a cost when the environment changes, because the evidence needed to detect and learn a new rule is less likely to be available.
Several limitations should be noted.
First, working memory reports provide an indirect measure of attentional priorities.
Differences in memory could arise during encoding, maintenance, or retrieval.
The present design cannot distinguish these stages.

Future work could combine working memory reports with eye tracking to examine how overt information sampling relates to what is subsequently retained, while varying probe timing to clarify when competing information becomes less available (Vogel et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Future work could combine working memory reports with eye tracking to examine how overt information sampling relates to what is subsequently retained, while varying probe timing to clarify when competing information becomes less available <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Vogel et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Second, rule certainty was inferred from participants' choices rather than directly measured or manipulated, and its effects on judgment and working memory were correlational.
Future work could incorporate confidence reports or manipulate the information available about the active rule, for example by changing feedback informativeness or providing partial rule cues.
This would help in assessing how model-derived certainty corresponds to participants' internal estimates across different levels of uncertainty, and how both relate to working memory prioritization.
In conclusion, the present findings suggest that learning what matters is accompanied by a reorganization of the information maintained in working memory.
As participants became more certain about which rule was active, memory increasingly favored goalrelevant over competing information, primarily through differences in estimated retention probability.
By combining computational estimates of rule beliefs with continuous working memory reports, the CARIT makes it possible to track how attentional priority changes as relevance is learned.
More broadly, this approach offers a window into how people align limited cognitive resources with evolving beliefs to support adaptive goal-directed behavior in dynamic environments.

text.text: Figure 1.
Continuously Assessed Rule Inference Task (CARIT).
(A) Three circular dimensions were each divided into two categories, defining six possible rules.
(B)Participants viewed stimuli defined by three continuous dimensions: color, shape, and motion.
On each trial, they judged whether the stimulus conformed to a hidden active rule and received binary feedback on their correctness.
Intermittent WM probes were placed randomly throughout the task to assess WM representation for all three dimensions of the previously seen stimulus.
Each probe was preceded by a pause symbol and followed by a play symbol, signaling that the probe did not change the active rule.
Participants responded on feature response wheels to reconstruct the color, shape, and motion of the previous stimulus.

Left axis: average rule judgment accuracy (blue).

Figure 3.

(A) Model-predicted RT as a function of rule certainty, at mean perceptual evidence and trial position.

(B) Model-predicted RT as a function of perceptual evidence on active and inactive dimensions, at each participant's mean certainty and controlling for trial position and evidence on the remaining dimensions.
(C) RT sensitivity to perceptual evidence (the slope of RT on prototype distance) as a function of rule certainty.
In B and C, active dimensions are shown in blue and inactive dimensions in gray, averaged across the two inactive dimensions.
